current.note: v18: hardware audit applied, 43 verified sources

dimensions.label: Discoverability
dimensions.desc: Can a first-time visitor tell what to do and find the interesting parts?

dimensions.label: Clarity
dimensions.desc: Is the content understandable to a 10-year-old and still useful to an enthusiast?

dimensions.label: Exploration
dimensions.desc: Depth of things to poke at: views, hotspots, angles, hidden layers.

dimensions.label: Delight
dimensions.desc: Is it fun? Motion, surprise, reward, personality.

dimensions.label: Feedback
dimensions.desc: Does every action respond immediately and legibly?

dimensions.label: Motion fidelity
dimensions.desc: How closely transitions follow the prototype video.

dimensions.label: Visual craft
dimensions.desc: Typography, hierarchy, polish, consistency with the Figma system.

dimensions.label: Accessibility
dimensions.desc: Keyboard, screen reader, contrast, reduced motion, touch targets.

dimensions.label: Mobile
dimensions.desc: Works and feels intentional on a phone.

dimensions.label: Performance
dimensions.desc: Load weight, frame rate, time to first interaction.

iterations.label: Figma baseline
iterations.summary: Faithful build of the V4 prototype + V5 style frames: flat renders, 4 view modes, 3 hotspots per part, fade/scan transitions.

critique.note: Nothing tells a first-timer they can hover hotspots or switch views; it reads as a poster.
Parts are flat PNGs — you can't turn them, zoom in, or look underneath. Three hotspots per part is the whole depth.
Four of seven parts are 'render in progress' dead ends.
The prototype video's language (pixel-mosaic intro, carousel slide, title ticker, typewriter, x-ray flash) is mostly missing.
Copy is pitched at enthusiasts. A 9-year-old won't know what 'parallel processing' means.
Callout text renders around 9–11px; grey #7d7d7d body copy on black is borderline contrast.
No reward for curiosity — nothing to find, collect, or play with.
Airflow legend and the connection web look interactive but do nothing.
Strong, faithful to Figma. Ghost type and HUD details carry the mood well.
Compact layout works, but hotspots are small and the art is cropped.

changes.desc: Static HTML/CSS/JS build of the Figma comps (session 1).

iterations.label: Real-time 3D + video motion
iterations.summary: Ported the Figma build to three.js with the three GLB models plus simplified stand-ins for the other four parts. Added the prototype video's motion language: 1-bit mosaic intro, carousel slide, title ticker, typewriter copy, light↔dark flash, top-down x-ray scan, drawn-on callouts, band-wipe home. New Airflow view, live power/data traces, clickable connection web, hotspot close-ups.

critique.note: Huge jump in what you can do, but nothing says so. A first-timer won't guess the part can be dragged, zoomed, or that hotspots fly in close.
Copy is still enthusiast-level ('vapor chamber', 'PCIe lanes'). A 9-year-old needs a plain-words layer and comparisons.
X-ray shows the inside, but you still can't pull a part apart. The GPU's named meshes (shroud, fans, heatsink, board) are begging for an exploded view.
The scan and airflow are genuinely fun. There is still no goal or reward for curiosity, and no sound.
The default hotspot can point at a feature turned away from you (GPU display ports), so the first callout appears dimmed and unexplained.
On phones the callout sits on top of the model and the hotspots are small for thumbs.
Renders every frame even when nothing moves; two copies of each mesh are drawn during scans.
Close to the video now. Missing: the glitch/noise exit and the copper render variant.
Keyboard + reduced-motion work; callout text is now 12–14px. The 3D view itself has no text alternative beyond its label.

changes.desc: three.js stage: GLB loading (meshopt + WebP), auto-centring/orientation, drag-to-spin with inertia, scroll/pinch zoom, idle sway.
Fresnel hologram twins revealed by a clipping-plane scan line; dense fins get a dimmer pass.
Power/Data show animated Manhattan-routed traces; new Airflow view with particle streams and faster fans.
Pixel-mosaic intro, carousel slide, title roll, erase-then-type copy, flash between light and dark, band wipe home.
All 7 parts explorable; RAM/SSD/cooler/PSU as labelled simplified models; motherboard hotspots anchored to real component materials (socket, RAM, M.2, CMOS battery, I/O).
Mode labels always visible; Airflow legend works; connection web is clickable.

iterations.label: Discoverability + plain words
iterations.summary: A first-visit tour that advances when you actually drag, tap a ring, switch view and change part; numbered hotspot rings with hover labels; Simple words by default with a More detail switch (copy written for 8–12 year olds for every part, view and hotspot); the starting hotspot is the one facing you; a phone callout card; ~30fps when idle and paused behind the index.

critique.note: Now easy to start, but there's still no reason to keep going. Kids love collecting: there are 24 features to find and nothing counts them.
X-ray hints at the inside, but you can't take the GPU apart. Its shroud, fans, heatsink and board are separate meshes — an exploded view is the obvious next step.
No sense of real size. A CPU on screen looks as big as a motherboard; kids need 'about the size of a cracker'.
Silent. A soft tick on switches and a whoosh on the x-ray scan would make actions feel physical (with a mute switch).
Hotspots are real buttons with labels and the wording switch helps reading levels; the 3D scene itself still has no text summary for screen readers.
The tour is quick and skippable and comes back via the ? button. Good.

changes.desc: 4-step coach marks (drag, tap a ring, switch view, change part) that move on when you do the thing; ? replays it.
Simple words / More detail switch; plain-language copy for 7 parts × up to 5 views + 24 hotspots, remembered between visits.
Numbered rings, hover labels, start on the feature facing you, explicit facing for GPU parts so close-ups turn the right way.
Callout moves into a card under the model; 40px touch rings.
Idle frames halved after 6s; rendering pauses behind the parts index.

iterations.label: Discoveries, size, sound
iterations.summary: Every hotspot you open is now a discovery: a ring counter in the header (n/24), check marks on found rings, toasts, a badge when a part is complete and a 'Computer Anatomist' finale. Real-world size comparisons under each part. Synthesized UI sounds (tick, slide whoosh, x-ray scan sweep, discovery chime) with a remembered mute. A live text summary of the 3D scene for screen readers. Close-ups zoom less on small parts.

critique.note: The last big missing idea: you still can't take a part apart. The GPU's shroud, fans, fins, board and backplate are separate meshes, and the stand-ins are built from parts — an exploded view would make 'anatomy' literal.
The header right side is getting busy (counter, sound, menu) and the bottom panel is dense at 1280px. Needs a calm pass.
Collecting works and the chime is satisfying. The finale card is static — the video's 1-bit mosaic would make it feel earned.
Still missing the video's glitch/noise exit.
Counter collapses to a ring on phones; check the header doesn't crowd at 360px.

changes.desc: Persistent found set (24 features), header progress ring, check-marked rings, toasts, per-part badge, all-found finale with reset.
Size comparison per part in Simple words; millimetres in More detail.
WebAudio synth sounds for tick, slide, scan, pop, discovery and badge; mute button remembered.
Screen-reader scene summary updates with each part/view; mute + counter have descriptive labels.
Zoom scales with part size so small parts don't fill the screen.

iterations.label: Exploded view
iterations.summary: 'Take it apart' peels each part into labelled layers: the GPU by its own named meshes (shroud, fans, fins, heat pipes, cold plate, board, backplate), the motherboard by component materials (memory, processor, covers, M.2, CMOS battery), the stand-ins by tagged pieces. Works in every view, so you can x-ray an exploded card. Labels relax so they don't overlap; tour gains a 'take it apart' step; E key toggles. Calmer layout: connection web drops out under 1280px. The finale now plays the intro's 1-bit circuit mosaic.

critique.note: You can now see how each part is built, but not how they fit together. The Figma sitemap's 'Assembly Guide / Ready to Build' branch is still missing — a guided build would give the whole site a goal.
Exploded labels are read-only; tapping a layer should say what it does.
The video's glitch exit is still missing on the way home.
Exploded labels get small on phones; still usable.
Exploded + x-ray together is the best-looking state in the site so far.

changes.desc: Per-piece rest/offset in part space converted to each piece's parent space; x-ray twins and edges follow their mesh; damped animation, side-on yaw and camera pull-back while apart.
Deduplicated layer labels projected each frame with overlap relaxation; hotspots hide while apart.
New 'take it apart' step; tour key bumped so returning visitors see it once.
Connection web hides below 1280px; explode button lives bottom-left of the stage.
All-found card plays the 1-bit mosaic behind it.

iterations.label: Guided build
iterations.summary: The Figma sitemap's 'Assembly Guide / Ready to Build' branch, as a game: 'Build a PC' empties the motherboard and asks six questions in assembly order (CPU, cooler, RAM, SSD, GPU, power). Pick the right part and it flies into its real position at real scale; a wrong pick shakes and gives a hint. Finishing switches the whole machine into the power x-ray. Also fixed: motherboard re-exported without palette merging, so CPU socket, CMOS battery and I/O hotspots anchor to the real components again; model URLs are versioned.

critique.note: The build gives the site a goal and teaches assembly order. It's a quiz, not a puzzle — dragging parts onto slots would be more hands-on, but tapping keeps it accessible for small kids and keyboards.
In the build, the board view is fixed; installed parts can hide the next slot (the GPU covers the lower board). A soft glow on the target slot would help.
The finished machine in power x-ray is a strong ending.
Build tray wraps to two rows on phones and the board is small; workable but cramped.
All three GLBs must load before the build can start; there's a toast if the board isn't ready, but no progress.

changes.desc: Six-step guided build with real-mm scaling (ATX = 305 mm), board-space orientations, drop-in animations, hints, and a power-on finale; Build again / Explore buttons.
Motherboard re-optimised without palette() — 45 named materials instead of 14 — restoring socket/battery/I/O anchors and exploded groups.
Versioned model URLs; ?build=N deep link; debug-only console hook.

iterations.label: Polish: slots, layers, glitch

You can switch parts and views from the keyboard but can't rotate or zoom the model without a mouse or touch.
Exploded GPU labels still bunch in the middle of the card; readable, not elegant.

iterations.label: Real models + drag-to-build
iterations.summary: Four new GLBs: the RAM, cooler and PSU stand-ins are replaced with real models, and a Corsair 4000D case joins as part eight (x-ray, airflow, take-apart, five hotspots). 'Build a PC' is now a workshop: drag each part from the bench into a cut-away case at real millimetre scale. It snaps onto a green hologram and clicks in. Every category has three options with live price, game speed, multitasking, memory, storage, power draw and CPU temperature. Hovering an option previews the difference, presets set a whole build, and power-on fails if the PSU is too small.

critique.note: Dragging a part until it snaps and clicks in, then powering on to RGB light and spinning fans, is the most game-like moment on the site. Kids get a goal, adults get a real cost/performance model.
Snap tick, 'Let go!' label, floating +$/−$ price tags, counting totals and colour-coded bars mean every action answers back.
In the whole-case view the CPU socket and M.2 slot are only ~40 px wide. A generous snap radius helps, but the camera should lean in toward small targets while you drag.
Touch dragging works and sideways swipes still scroll the bench, but with the spec strip on top the case gets only about a third of a phone screen.
Every option in a category reuses one model (only its size changes), and the SSD is still a simplified stand-in. Both need new GLBs from the owner.

iterations.label: Figma prototype build
iterations.summary: A new track beside the live build: the final motion mockup (the 23-second EIII P2 video) as a working site on the Figma record's framework, using the real 3D models. It follows the V5.04.01 layout: grayscale photo parts on the white-to-black gradient, title and copy in the footer, a part switcher and side arrows. The motion follows the video: the 1-bit circuit intro; the first part drifting in as the title dissolves; copy eaten from its first letter while parts slide and the title ticks; rings fading in; dissolves into a cyan x-ray with the printing glowing; ruled callouts; a warm scan wipe into a 1-bit pan through the machine; and a glitch to black. The Figma prototype page supplies Overview/Framework/Power/Data with '(1) down, (2) up', plus a parts index.

critique.note: Side by side with the video, each beat lands within a few frames: start drift, carousel and title tick, copy erase and type, ring fade, x-ray dissolve with the callout after it, exit wipes, 1-bit pan, glitch.
The x-ray is unlit glow that adds light without writing alpha, and printed text lights up by its edges, so 'RTX 3080' and 'RYZEN' read as in the comps.
Deliberately stays within the mockup's scope (8 parts × 4 views + hotspots). Take-apart, glossary and the drag-to-build workshop live in the live build.
The mockup's CPU is an AM5 Ryzen 9 7950X3D; the only CPU model available is the AM4 Ryzen 5 3600.

iterations.label: Researched power + data paths
iterations.summary: Every part's Power and Data views are now labelled maps of the real component, built from manufacturer specs and datasheets. A shared module draws each path between named components (taken from the model where it names them, otherwise placed from board layouts and teardowns), with parallel traces for buses, arrows for direction, and on-screen labels: plain names by default, voltages, bus widths and speeds in 'More detail'. iterations.label: Real wires, sound, narrative
iterations.summary: The power and data maps became real wiring: copper pours for power and thin copper traces for data on every board (45° bends, length-matched DDR serpentines, differential pairs, gold pads), and insulated harnesses in the ATX colour code with connector housings wherever a cable runs (24-pin and EPS into the board, the GPU's 12-pin, the case's harnesses behind the tray, the fan cable, the PSU's mains and DC leads on a bare main board). Light travels inside the copper and insulation; each view draws its wiring on from the source end. Three workers shaped the round: narrative direction ('Follow the Power': the live build now opens on the PSU and runs energy → information → heat, with 26 copy edits), style (an angiogram look, A minor, air not electronics, motion fixes) and hardware accuracy. The stock blips were replaced by a generative A-minor score that adds a layer per view, and real recorded whooshes and taps (CC0 / Pixabay licence, credited).

critique.note: Wiring reads as physical: real conductor colours, connector housings, cables that stay visible (unlit) in the other view.

changes.desc: flowmap.js rebuilt as a wiring renderer (pour, trace, pairs, ddr, cable) with PBR copper, PVC and nylon; harness.js holds conductor-by-conductor cable specs.
sfx.js: generative A-minor score with per-view layers, ducking, tab-hidden fade, tape-stop exit; six recorded sounds in their roles; prototype gains sound and an M / index switch.

iterations.label: Hardware audit applied
iterations.summary: The hardware-accuracy worker's audit (55 sources researched, 43 verified and published) is applied. Corrections: the 4000D ships with one front and one rear fan; the Z370-E's VRM is 10 phases and its memory and chipset rails come from board regulators, not straight from the 24-pin; the RTX 3080 FE has a vapour chamber, 15 + 3 power phases and ten separate 32-bit memory links; the 980 PRO has no sourced PMIC, so the copy now says regulators, with real NAND and DRAM speeds; the PSU's transformer is drawn as an isolation gap that no copper crosses (an opto-coupler carries on/off), at 380–400 V; the 7950X3D gets its two NVMe x4 links and a PCIe 4.0 chipset link; and the case gains the reset lead, a flat black USB 3.0 cable, a separate USB-C cable and a second 8-pin feed for the GPU adapter. The 24-pin harness now includes the brown 3.3 V sense wire in pin 13. Unsourced PSU-internal cables became board copper. Dead AnandTech links were swapped for archived copies.

critique.note: Every number on the maps now traces to a verified source on credits.html; unverifiable or paywalled sources are left off.
Still open: the live CPU is an AM4 Ryzen 5 3600 beside an LGA1151 board (I-53); the copy now notes PCIe 3.0 on this board for the GPU and SSD.

changes.desc: Copy, nodes, link kinds and harnesses corrected from data/direction/hardware.md and wiring.json.
New 'field' link kind for isolation gaps; harnesses can carry a second wire per pin; reset, flat USB 3.0 and USB-C cables.

timeline.text: Revisit the Elements III P2 Figma file and code a working website from its iterations.
Mapped 17 Figma pages: wireframes, V1–V5 comps, prototype, final style frames (video timecodes).
Final direction = V5 style frames (greyscale, AoC header) + V4 prototype interactions (4 view modes).
Pulled design context + 32 assets (icons, renders, circuit textures) from Figma.
Static site built: intro, 7-part carousel, 4 view modes, hotspots, index overlay, compact layout.
Verified desktop + mobile in browser pane; fixed letterbox, ghost text, deep links.
Heavy task: 3D progress matrix, video-driven motion, GLB models, critique-and-improve loop; keep a Figma record + a live version.
Broke the 23s prototype video into 92 frames; wrote a motion spec (pixel-mosaic intro, carousel slide, title ticker, typewriter, x-ray flash, band wipe, glitch out).
Optimised GLBs 31.4 MB → 3.0 MB (meshopt geometry, WebP textures, motherboard flattened + instanced).
Froze Figma build as /baseline; live iterations go in /live; progress recorder feeds /matrix.
Testing headless screenshots of the Figma baseline
v0 recorded: Figma baseline
Building the 3D progress matrix (score grid, issue arcs, code skyline, chat helix)
3D build matrix online: score grid, issue arcs, code skyline, chat helix, screenshot cards, live beacon (polls every 3s).
Porting the site to real-time 3D: loading the three GLB models into the Figma layout
Tuning model orientation, x-ray look and hotspot anchors; reviewing every part and view
v1 recorded: Real-time 3D + video motion
v1 critique: biggest gaps are discoverability (no cues) and clarity for kids. v2 = onboarding coach, Simple/Detailed copy, facing-aware default hotspot, phone callout card, idle frame throttle.
Writing plain-language copy for 7 parts x 5 views + 26 hotspots; building the coach-mark tour
v2 recorded: Discoverability + plain words

v2 critique: easy to start, no reason to keep going. v3 = discovery tracker with badges, real-world size comparisons, synthesized UI sound + mute, screen-reader scene summary. Exploded view held for v4.
Building the discovery tracker (24 features), badges, size comparisons and WebAudio sound
v3 recorded: Discoveries, size, sound

v3 critique: the missing idea is taking parts apart. v4 = exploded view (GPU by its named meshes, motherboard by component materials, stand-ins by tagged pieces) with layer labels; calmer layout; mosaic finale.
Building the exploded view: layering GPU nodes, lifting motherboard components, tagging stand-in pieces
v4 recorded: Exploded view
Designing the guided build (Figma 'Assembly Guide'): install parts onto the motherboard in the right order
v5 recorded: Guided build
Critiquing the 3D matrix itself: clutter, label overload, what the data is actually saying
Matrix v2: stretched colour ramp, screenshot wall above the bars, elevated camera, per-dimension sparklines with click-to-highlight, time-by-phase, headline trend. Added a hub page at the root.
Polish round: build slot glow, tappable exploded labels, glitch exit, phone build tray, perf (no rendering behind the intro)
v6 recorded: Polish: slots, layers, glitch
Promote the guided build up front; keyboard rotate/zoom; power-on finale
v7 recorded: Build up front + keyboard 3D
v7 recorded: Build up front + keyboard 3D
Caught a syntax error from my own one-line comment after recording v7; fixed, re-checked with tools/check.sh, re-recorded v7. New rule: check.sh runs before every recording.
v7 recorded: Build up front + keyboard 3D
Holistic visual review at laptop size; calm pass on panel density and header
v8 recorded: Calm pass + preload
Building the Glossary (Figma 'Quick Reference') and a full-screen 3D view for phones
v9 recorded: Glossary + full-screen 3D
End-to-end QA: phone flows, keyboard-only, reduced motion
v10 recorded: QA round
Size line-up (Figma 'Compare Specs'): every part side by side at real scale
v11 recorded: Size line-up
Final review of the matrix and live site; deciding whether another round is worth it

Stopping the loop at v11: every branch of the Figma sitemap exists, all 35 logged issues are fixed, and the remaining levers are new content (real GLBs for the four stand-ins, a case) or adding a build step for performance — owner decisions, not UX fixes.
12 iterations, avg UX score 5.3 → 9.1, 35/35 issues fixed. Figma record at /baseline, live build at /live, this matrix at /matrix.
New models (case, PSU, RAM, cooler) + drag parts into a PC case, with options, live price total and spec differences
Optimised 4 new GLBs (27 MB to 3 MB); building the case workshop
Workshop tested: drag, snap, touch, keyboard, power-on, PSU failure; recording v12
v12 recorded: Real models + drag-to-build
v13 recorded: Lean-in drag + phone room
v13: lean-in drag, phone room, lighter case model
Build out the Figma record prototype with the 3D models, using the framework and motion of the Figma file and the final motion mockup video
Mockup studied beat by beat; prototype built and compared frame by frame
